vjimc-2005-cat2-01.title: Two nilpotent matrices
vjimc-2005-cat2-01.body:
If $A$ and $B$ commute, the usual Cauchy-product argument gives $\exp(A+B)=\exp(A)\exp(B)$, so we need non-commuting matrices. Take
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $A^2=B^2=0$, so
$$\exp(A)=I+A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad\exp(B)=I+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad \exp(A)\exp(B)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
On the other hand $A+B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $(A+B)^2=I$, so $(A+B)^k=I$ for even $k$ and $=A+B$ for odd $k$. Hence
$$\exp(A+B)=\Big(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac1{(2k)!}\Big)I+\Big(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac1{(2k+1)!}\Big)(A+B)=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh1&\sinh1\\\sinh1&\cosh1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Since $\cosh 1\approx1.543\ne2$, $\exp(A+B)\ne\exp(A)\exp(B)$. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat2-01.title: A projection and a nilpotent
vjimc-2005-cat2-01.body:
Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^k=A$ for $k\ge1$ and $B^2=0$, so
$$\exp(A)=I+(e-1)A=\begin{pmatrix}e&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad \exp(B)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad\exp(A)\exp(B)=\begin{pmatrix}e&e\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Now $C=A+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $C^2=C$, hence $\exp(C)=I+(e-1)C=\begin{pmatrix}e&e-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which differs from $\exp(A)\exp(B)$ in the top-right entry. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat2-02.title: Take a maximising set
vjimc-2005-cat2-02.body:
For $I\subset\{1,\dots,n\}$ let $F(I)=\sum_{i\in I,j\notin I}a_{i,j}+\sum_{i\notin I,j\in I}a_{i,j}$ (the "cut" entries). Choose $\mathcal J$ with $F(\mathcal J)$ maximal.

For $k\in\mathcal J$, moving $k$ out of $\mathcal J$ does not increase $F$. Only entries in row $k$ or column $k$ change status ($a_{k,k}=0$ plays no role):
$$0\le F(\mathcal J)-F(\mathcal J\setminus\{k\})=\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}a_{k,j}+\sum_{i\notin\mathcal J}a_{i,k}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}a_{k,j}-\sum_{i\in\mathcal J}a_{i,k}.$$
Summing over $k\in\mathcal J$, the positive part gives exactly $F(\mathcal J)$ and the negative part gives $2\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal J}a_{i,j}$. Hence
$$\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal J}a_{i,j}\le\tfrac12F(\mathcal J).$$
Similarly, for $k\notin\mathcal J$ comparing with $\mathcal J\cup\{k\}$ and summing over $k\notin\mathcal J$ gives
$$\sum_{i,j\notin\mathcal J}a_{i,j}\le\tfrac12F(\mathcal J).$$
Every entry is either in one of the two diagonal blocks or is cut, so
$$\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^na_{i,j}=\frac12\Big(\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal J}a_{i,j}+\sum_{i,j\notin\mathcal J}a_{i,j}+F(\mathcal J)\Big)\le\frac12\Big(\tfrac12F(\mathcal J)+\tfrac12F(\mathcal J)+F(\mathcal J)\Big)=F(\mathcal J). \qquad ∎$$

vjimc-2005-cat2-02.title: Averaging over random sets
vjimc-2005-cat2-02.body:
Choose $\mathcal J$ at random: each index is put in $\mathcal J$ independently with probability $\frac12$. For $i\ne j$ the entry $a_{i,j}$ is counted in $F(\mathcal J)$ exactly when one of $i,j$ is in $\mathcal J$ and the other is not, which has probability $\frac12$. The diagonal entries are $0$. By linearity of expectation,
$$\mathbb E\,F(\mathcal J)=\sum_{i\ne j}\tfrac12a_{i,j}=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j=1}^na_{i,j}.$$
A random variable cannot always be smaller than its mean, so some $\mathcal J$ satisfies $F(\mathcal J)\ge\frac12\sum_{i,j}a_{i,j}$. (Without probability: the average of $F(I)$ over all $2^n$ subsets $I$ equals $\frac12\sum a_{i,j}$, so the maximum is at least that.) ∎

vjimc-2005-cat2-03.title: Polynomials first, then Weierstrass approximation
vjimc-2005-cat2-03.body:
Put $Q=[0,1]^2$ and $L_n(f)=\Big(\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}\Big)^2\iint_Q\big(xy(1-x)(1-y)\big)^nf(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. $L_n$ is linear and positive ($f\ge0\Rightarrow L_n(f)\ge0$).

**Step 1: monomials.** The Beta integral (repeated integration by parts) gives $\int_0^1x^{p}(1-x)^{n}dx=\frac{p!\,n!}{(p+n+1)!}$. Hence
$$L_n(x^ky^l)=\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}\cdot\frac{(n+k)!\,n!}{(2n+k+1)!}\cdot\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}\cdot\frac{(n+l)!\,n!}{(2n+l+1)!}=\prod_{i=1}^k\frac{n+i}{2n+1+i}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^l\frac{n+i}{2n+1+i}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac1{2^k}\cdot\frac1{2^l}.$$
In particular $L_n(1)=1$, and $L_n(x^ky^l)\to\big(\frac12\big)^k\big(\frac12\big)^l$.

**Step 2: polynomials.** By linearity, $L_n(P)\to P(\frac12,\frac12)$ for every polynomial $P(x,y)$.

**Step 3: continuous $f$.** Let $\varepsilon>0$. By the Weierstrass (Stone–Weierstrass) approximation theorem there is a polynomial $P$ with $|f-P|<\varepsilon$ on $Q$. By positivity and $L_n(1)=1$, $|L_n(f)-L_n(P)|\le L_n(|f-P|)\le\varepsilon$. By Step 2 there is $n_0$ with $|L_n(P)-P(\frac12,\frac12)|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge n_0$. Then for $n\ge n_0$
$$\Big|L_n(f)-f\big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\big)\Big|\le|L_n(f)-L_n(P)|+\Big|L_n(P)-P\big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\big)\Big|+\Big|P\big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\big)-f\big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\big)\Big|<3\varepsilon .$$
**Answer:** the limit is $f\big(\frac12,\frac12\big)$. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat2-03.title: Concentration of the kernel
vjimc-2005-cat2-03.body:
Let $p_n(x)=\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}\big(x(1-x)\big)^n$. By the Beta integral $\int_0^1p_n=1$, and the integral in question is $\iint_Q p_n(x)p_n(y)f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$, where $K_n(x,y)=p_n(x)p_n(y)\ge0$ has total integral $1$.

**$p_n$ is small away from $\frac12$.** Since $\binom{2n}{n}\le4^n$, we have $\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}=(2n+1)\binom{2n}n\le(2n+1)4^n$. If $|x-\frac12|\ge\delta$ then $x(1-x)=\frac14-(x-\frac12)^2\le\frac14-\delta^2$, so
$$p_n(x)\le(2n+1)(1-4\delta^2)^n\to0\quad\text{uniformly on }\{|x-\tfrac12|\ge\delta\}.$$
Hence the mass of $K_n$ outside the square $U_\delta=\{|x-\frac12|<\delta,|y-\frac12|<\delta\}$ is at most $\int_{|x-1/2|\ge\delta}p_n+\int_{|y-1/2|\ge\delta}p_n\le 2(2n+1)(1-4\delta^2)^n\to0$.

**Conclusion.** Let $\varepsilon>0$, $M=\max|f|$, and by continuity choose $\delta$ with $|f(x,y)-f(\frac12,\frac12)|<\varepsilon$ on $U_\delta$. Then
$$\Big|\iint_QK_nf-f\big(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\big)\Big|=\Big|\iint_QK_n\big(f-f(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\big)\Big|\le\varepsilon\iint_{U_\delta}K_n+2M\iint_{Q\setminus U_\delta}K_n\le\varepsilon+4M(2n+1)(1-4\delta^2)^n,$$
which is $<2\varepsilon$ for large $n$. So the limit is $f(\frac12,\frac12)$. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat2-04.title: Squares form an additive subgroup
vjimc-2005-cat2-04.body:
Let $S=\{x^2:x\in R\}$. The hypothesis says $S+S\subseteq S$.

**$S$ is an additive subgroup.** $0=0^2\in S$. Fix $y\in S$. The map $S\to S$, $x\mapsto x+y$, is injective, and $S$ is finite, so it is surjective. Thus for every $s\in S$ there is $x\in S$ with $x+y=s$, i.e. $s-y\in S$. So $S$ is closed under subtraction.

**Anticommutators are in $S$.** For any $x,y\in R$,
$$xy+yx=(x+y)^2-x^2-y^2\in S .$$

**Conclusion.** For arbitrary $a,b,c\in R$, apply this (using associativity) with
$$x=a,\ y=bc:\quad abc+bca\in S;\qquad x=c,\ y=ab:\quad cab+abc\in S;\qquad x=ca,\ y=b:\quad cab+bca\in S .$$
Adding the first two and subtracting the third gives $2abc\in S$, i.e. $2abc=d^2$ for some $d\in R$. ∎
